Sup A: bolton_2006_cake_complete_blocking · Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids (Cake-complete blocking)
The paper develops five combined fouling models for membrane filtration, including a cake-complete model for protein solutions filtered through microporous membranes. The model represents fouling through both growth of a cake layer and loss of open membrane area, and predicts permeate volume over time at constant pressure or pressure over time at constant flow. It uses Darcy’s law and two fitted parameters, and approaches the individual cake or complete-blocking models when one mechanism dominates. The authors tested it using sterile filtration of human plasma IgG and virus filtration of BSA, as well as constant-flow IgG tests, in bench-scale membrane holders. They compared its fits with individual and other combined fouling models and considered its use for membrane-area sizing.
comparison: The authors describe their combined models as less physically detailed than Ho and Zydney et al. (2000), but simpler to implement numerically.
comparison: The four individual fouling mechanisms used as components are the classical mechanisms cited to Grace (1956) and Hermia (1982).
comparison: The paper compares the combined models with the earlier pore-blockage and cake-filtration model of Ho and Zydney et al. (2000), which used three fitted parameters.
data: Five constant-pressure BSA runs used 47 mm holders, and permeate volume was measured until flux had fallen 98% from an initial 3.58 × 10⁻⁴ m/s.
data: The BSA results were averaged across the five runs, with standard deviation calculated at each time point.
data: The experimental system collected filtration data every second for one hour.
data: Three constant-flow IgG experiments measured pressure over time while solution was pumped through 47 mm holders at 579 L m⁻² h⁻¹.
data: Three constant-pressure IgG experiments used 13 mm holders, and permeate volume was measured until flux had fallen 95% from an initial 1.13 × 10⁻³ m/s.
equipment: Constant-pressure tests used a pressure vessel, stainless-steel membrane holders, an electronic balance, and a digital pressure gauge.
fitting: For the standard-model comparison in the constant-pressure IgG analysis, only the standard-blocking constant was fitted to avoid refitting the initial flux for each experiment.
fitting: Model fits were assessed by minimizing the sum of squared residuals between measured points and model predictions.
fitting: The paper reports fitted point estimates and fit errors but does not report parameter confidence intervals or other parameter-uncertainty estimates.
inputs: The formulation takes initial flux, initial membrane area, elapsed time, and initial pressure as inputs, and has no state variables.
interpretation: A good fit from the cake-complete model does not establish that pore blockage and cake formation actually occurred simultaneously.
interpretation: Because the mechanisms may be coupled, the fitted cake and blocking parameters can represent average values over the filtration run.
materials: BSA was prepared at 2.5 mg/mL in pH 7.2 PBS, and human plasma IgG was prepared at 10.0 mg/mL in pH 7.2 PBS.
mechanism: Cake filtration represents particles accumulating on the membrane surface in a permeable layer that adds flow resistance.
mechanism: Complete blocking represents particles sealing pore entrances so those pores no longer carry flow.
mechanism: In the cake-complete model, cake forms on the area that remains unblocked, and blockage removes membrane area from flow.
mechanism: The cake-complete model idealizes caking and complete blocking as independent effects, although the paper notes that they may interact in real filtration.
operation: The BSA virus-filtration tests used Viresolve 180, a composite PVDF membrane, at 30 psi.
operation: The IgG sterile-filtration tests used a nominal 0.22 μm Durapore PVDF membrane at 10 psi.
operation: The constant-pressure equipment used 13 or 47 mm stainless-steel holders and four 600 mL chambers connected to the pressure source.
outputs: At constant flow, the model predicts pressure as a function of time.
outputs: At constant pressure, the model predicts permeate volume as a function of time.
outputs: When one mechanism contributes little, the combined model reduces to the corresponding individual cake-filtration or complete-blocking model.
results: For constant-flow IgG filtration, the cake-intermediate model had the lowest SSR at 0.58, while the cake-complete model had an SSR of 1.36.
results: For constant-pressure BSA filtration, the cake-intermediate model fit best with an SSR of 959, compared with 1,620 for the cake-complete model, and the two fits were within the standard deviation of most data points.
results: For constant-pressure IgG filtration, the cake-complete model had an SSR of 11.2, slightly lower than the standard model’s 13.9.
results: The cake-complete model could closely reproduce predictions from each of the four individual fouling models.
scope: The authors present the cake-complete model as useful for curves whose flux decline lies between the cake-filtration and complete-blocking extremes.
scope: The cake-standard and cake-intermediate models are intended for cases where those combinations agree with experimentally observed fouling mechanisms.
scope: The model does not provide a direct formula for permeate volume at a specified flux decline, so that quantity must be found numerically.
structure: The combined fouling relations were derived using Darcy’s law.
structure: The model uses two fitted parameters, one for cake filtration and one for complete blocking.
structure: The supplied formulation has eight algebraic laws and no state variables, so its time-dependent predictions are calculated from relations rather than state ODEs.
system: The experimental streams were BSA for virus filtration and human plasma IgG for sterile filtration.
system: The model describes fouling during filtration of protein solutions through microporous membranes.
use: The authors propose the cake-complete model as useful for membrane-area sizing.

Sup B: ho_2000 · A Combined Pore Blockage and Cake Filtration Model for Protein Fouling during Microfiltration
The model describes protein fouling during microfiltration of bovine serum albumin solutions through polycarbonate membranes. It predicts how filtrate flow and flux decline over time as protein aggregates first cover open membrane areas and a protein deposit then grows over the covered regions. The full model combines flow through uncovered and covered areas and accounts for differences in deposit resistance according to when each region was first covered; the authors also derive a simpler approximate solution. Experiments were run in a stirred cell at constant pressure, with BSA concentration and pressure varied, and the model was compared with measured flux and collected filtrate volume. The authors use it to explain the transition from pore blockage to cake filtration and other observed flux-decline patterns, and to investigate the mechanisms of protein fouling.
availability: The paper does not state that model code or experimental data are publicly available.
data: Deposited protein mass was measured by weighing a dry membrane before and after filtration and air drying it for 12 h.
data: Filtrate flow rate was measured by timed collection on a digital balance, and total collected filtrate volume was reported.
data: Repeat experiments differed by less than 10%.
data: The authors assessed deposit resistance by filtering 2 g/L BSA for 5 h at 14 kPa, then measuring saline flow through the rinsed membrane at several pressures.
data: The initial flux varied between 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ and 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s across the membranes in the concentration-series experiments.
equipment: Filtration experiments used a 25-mm-diameter stirred ultrafiltration cell connected to an air-pressurized acrylic solution reservoir.
equipment: The membranes were 0.2-μm polycarbonate track-etched membranes.
fitting: The approximate solution gave results only slightly below those from the full model in the concentration-series comparisons.
fitting: The concentration-series model calculations agreed with both flux and filtrate-volume data over the full time interval using one parameter set.
fitting: The full numerical model tended to underestimate total resistance at long times, and a slightly larger cake-growth resistance rate improved that agreement.
mechanism: The authors interpret the deposit resistance as depending on solution conditions such as pH and ionic strength.
mechanism: The combined formulation gives a smooth transition from pore blockage to cake filtration without requiring separate mathematical descriptions for the two regimes.
mechanism: The model predicts that cake growth is self-leveling because high-resistance regions have lower flux and therefore grow more slowly.
mechanism: The model represents early fouling as aggregate blockage and later fouling as growth of a protein cake or deposit over covered regions.
model: The authors also develop an approximate analytical solution that assumes uniform resistance over the fouled membrane area.
model: The full model is dynamic and predicts filtrate flow over the course of filtration.
model: The full model uses three evolving quantities: uncovered membrane area, deposit mass per area, and deposit resistance.
model: The model accounts for spatially varying deposit resistance by integrating over regions that were blocked at different times.
model: The model adds the flow through open membrane regions to the flow through blocked regions.
operation: BSA solutions were prepared in phosphate-buffered saline adjusted to pH 7.4, freshly prepared before each run, and used within 8 h.
operation: The cell was first run with saline until its flux reached steady state, then rapidly emptied and refilled with BSA solution before repressurization.
operation: The concentration series comprised five BSA solutions ranging from 0.5 to 5 g/L, filtered at 14 kPa.
operation: The pressure series filtered 2 g/L BSA at transmembrane pressures spanning 5.5 to 55 kPa (0.8 to 8 psi).
operation: The stirred-cell experiments were conducted at room temperature, reported as 22 ± 2°C.
parameters: For the concentration series, the three fitted quantities were obtained by minimizing squared residuals using steepest descent.
parameters: For the pressure series, the blockage parameter was taken from the concentration-series fit while the other two quantities were fitted separately at each pressure.
parameters: The flux fits estimate three fouling quantities: the blockage parameter, initial deposit resistance, and the product of deposition fraction and specific layer resistance.
parameters: The reported parameter standard deviations were obtained from the optimization routine.
prior work: Mochizuki and Zydney (1993) supplied a literature estimate of BSA-deposit specific surface area used to estimate initial deposit resistance.
prior work: The aggregate fraction and aggregate size used for an independent estimate of the blockage parameter came from Ho and Zydney (1999).
prior work: The observed transition between early blockage and later cake filtration is discussed in relation to Tracey and Davis (1994) and Bowen et al. (1995).
prior work: The paper contrasts its combined approach with Kelly and Zydney (1995), who used a modified pore-blockage model for BSA fouling.
prior work: The paper places classical pore-blockage, pore-constriction, and cake-filtration descriptions in the common framework of Hermans and Bredée (1936) and Gonsalves (1950).
prior work: The paper relates its cake-compressibility description to power-law approaches used by Porter (1977) and Belter et al. (1988).
results: At 32 min the average deposit resistance over covered regions was 6% below the maximum, and after 100 min it was less than 3% below the maximum.
results: At 8 min in the 2 g/L run, 74% of the membrane area was covered but only 6% of the filtrate flow passed through fouled regions.
results: The model explains a maximum in the flux-decline diagnostic that earlier work had observed without a mechanical explanation.
results: The short-time flux-decline plot had a measured log-log slope of 2.0 ± 0.1, consistent with classical complete pore blocking.
results: The total resistance continued to increase after 100 min at the highest tested protein concentration, so flux did not reach steady state under those conditions.
scope: The authors present the model as describing protein flux decline through membranes with noninterconnected pore structures.
scope: The protein-deposit resistance increased with applied pressure, which the authors attribute to compression of the BSA deposit.
system: The authors describe BSA aggregates as forming through intermolecular disulfide bonds between albumin molecules.
system: The model describes bovine serum albumin (BSA) protein fouling during membrane microfiltration.
system: The paper attributes much of the membrane-surface deposition to large protein aggregates.
use: The authors intend the model to explain flux behavior over the complete filtration process and provide insight into protein-fouling mechanisms.

answer.description: A and B both model protein fouling during membrane filtration by combining pore blockage with cake formation, and both are compared with BSA filtration data under constant pressure. B represents blockage followed by deposit growth over covered regions, with evolving membrane coverage and spatially varying deposit resistance. A is a simpler combined model that treats cake formation and complete blockage as independent effects, using two fitted parameters and algebraic relations rather than evolving state variables. A’s paper specifically compares its simpler approach with B.
